q: Match each country with a dish it is famous for.
fact: Rösti, a crispy cake of grated potato, began as a farmers' breakfast in the Swiss canton of Bern.

q: Match each Asian country with one of its best-known dishes.
fact: Nasi lemak is rice cooked in coconut milk. 'Lemak' means rich or creamy in Malay.

q: Match each South American country with a hearty dish that comes from it.
fact: Feijoada is a slow-cooked stew of black beans and pork. In Brazil it is a classic Saturday lunch.

q: Match each African country with a dish that is a favorite there.
fact: Doro wat, a spicy chicken stew, is eaten with injera bread and is the centerpiece of Ethiopian holiday meals.

q: Match each European country with a food it is known for.
fact: The Sachertorte was created in Vienna in 1832 by Franz Sacher, a 16-year-old apprentice cook.

q: Match each country with a famous landmark found there.
fact: Big Ben is really the name of the great bell inside the clock tower in London, not of the tower itself.

q: Match each Asian country with a landmark found there.
fact: The Golden Temple in Amritsar is the holiest shrine of Sikhism. Its free kitchen serves meals to tens of thousands of visitors a day.

q: Match each country in the Americas with a landmark found there.
fact: Teotihuacan's Pyramid of the Sun, near Mexico City, is one of the largest pyramids in the world.

q: Match each African country with a landmark found there.
fact: In the 1960s the temples of Abu Simbel were cut into huge blocks and rebuilt higher up, to save them from the waters of a new dam.

q: Match each country of Oceania with a famous sight found there.
fact: Despite its name, Milford Sound in New Zealand is a fiord, carved out by glaciers rather than by a river.

q: Match each country with its national animal.
fact: The takin, Bhutan's national animal, looks like a cross between a goat and a cow.

q: Match each country with its national bird.
fact: The rufous hornero builds a clay nest shaped like an old-fashioned oven - 'horno' in Spanish.

q: Match each country with a sport that was invented there.
fact: Korfball, invented in Amsterdam in 1902, was designed for mixed teams of men and women playing together.

q: Match each European river with the sea it flows into.
fact: The Rhine reaches the North Sea through a wide delta in the Netherlands, which it shares with the Meuse.

q: Match each great river with the sea at its mouth.
fact: The Indus, which gave India its name, flows mostly through Pakistan.

q: Match each peak with the mountain range it belongs to.
fact: Mount Whitney, at about 4,420 meters, is the highest peak in the United States outside Alaska.

q: Match each European country with its highest mountain.
fact: Spain's highest peak, Teide, is not on the mainland at all but on the island of Tenerife.

q: Match each African country with its highest mountain.
fact: Toubkal, in the Atlas Mountains, is the highest peak in North Africa at about 4,170 meters.

q: Match each European capital with the river it stands on.
fact: The Tagus is the longest river of the Iberian Peninsula. It rises in Spain and reaches the sea at Lisbon.

q: Match each country with a musical instrument from its traditions.
fact: A didgeridoo is traditionally made from a eucalyptus branch that termites have hollowed out.

q: Match each country with an instrument of its traditional music.
fact: The angklung, made of bamboo tubes that rattle when shaken, is on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage.

q: Match each explorer with what he was the first European to reach.
fact: Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488. Ten years later Vasco da Gama sailed on around it and reached India.

q: Match each pioneer with the first they achieved.
pairs: First to walk on the Moon
fact: Junko Tabei of Japan reached the top of Everest in 1975, 22 years after the first ascent.

q: Match each country with its currency.
fact: Poland's zloty simply means 'golden'.

q: Match each European country with its own currency.
fact: Romania's leu means 'lion', a name taken from old Dutch coins that showed a lion and once circulated there.

q: Match each Latin American country with its currency.
fact: Costa Rica's colón is named after Christopher Columbus, who is called Cristóbal Colón in Spanish.

q: Match each country with its national language.
fact: Filipino is based on Tagalog, the language of Manila and the region around it.

q: Match each country with one of its official languages.
fact: Quechua was the language of the Inca Empire and is still spoken by millions of people in the Andes.

q: Match each country with its most celebrated writer.
fact: Spanish is often called 'the language of Cervantes', just as English is 'the language of Shakespeare'.

q: Match each country with a famous painter born there.
fact: Hokusai's woodblock print 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa' is one of the most famous images in the world.

q: Match each country with a great composer born there.
fact: Dvořák wrote his famous 'New World' Symphony while he was living in the United States, in 1893.

q: Match each country with an invention that was made there.
fact: Swiss engineer George de Mestral got the idea for Velcro from burrs that stuck to his dog's fur on a walk.

q: Match each country with a company founded there.
fact: Nokia began in 1865 as a paper mill in Finland and only later turned to rubber boots, cables and phones.

q: Match each country with its national flower.
fact: South Africa's cricket team, the Proteas, is named after the national flower.

q: Match each country with the symbol at the heart of its flag.
fact: The red and blue circle on South Korea's flag, the taegeuk, stands for balance. Four black trigrams surround it.

q: Match each country with the emblem shown on its flag.
fact: Lesotho's flag shows a mokorotlo, the cone-shaped straw hat of the Basotho people.

q: Match each country with a lake that lies within it.
fact: Issyk-Kul lies high in the mountains yet never freezes. Its name means 'warm lake'.

q: Match each country with an animal that lives in the wild only there.
fact: New Zealand's kakapo is the world's only flightless parrot, and also the heaviest parrot of all.

q: Match each country with a city that used to be its capital.
fact: Kazakhstan moved its capital from Almaty to Astana in 1997, partly to bring it closer to the center of the country.

q: Match each country with its largest city - none of them is the capital.
fact: Switzerland's constitution names no capital at all. Bern is officially called the 'federal city'.

q: Match each city with its famous nickname.
fact: Jaipur's old city was painted pink to welcome the Prince of Wales in 1876, and has stayed that way.

q: Match each country with an ancient civilization that was centered there.
fact: The Minoans of Crete built the great palace of Knossos, linked to the legend of the Minotaur.

q: Match each African country with the European country it became independent from.
fact: DR Congo, which became independent from Belgium in 1960, is about 75 times larger than Belgium.

q: Match each city with a name it once went by.
fact: Oslo was called Christiania, after the Danish-Norwegian King Christian IV, for about 300 years until 1925.

q: Match each city with its name in colonial times.
fact: Kinshasa took its present name in 1966. It is now one of the largest cities in Africa.

q: Match each country with a sports legend who represented it.
fact: Pelé is the only player to have won the World Cup three times, in 1958, 1962 and 1970.

q: Match each country with a champion who comes from it.
fact: Magnus Carlsen became world chess champion in 2013 and held the title until 2023, when he chose not to defend it.

q: Match each country with the nickname of its national football team.
fact: Bafana Bafana means 'the boys, the boys' in Zulu.

q: Match each country with the nickname of its national rugby team.
fact: Tonga's Ikale Tahi means 'sea eagles'. Like New Zealand's haka, Pacific teams perform a traditional challenge before kickoff.

q: Match each country with a word people use to say hello there.
fact: Kia ora, a Māori greeting used all over New Zealand, literally wishes someone good health.

q: Match each country with its traditional dress.
fact: Many Norwegians wear their bunad, a regional folk costume, on Constitution Day, May 17.

q: Match each country with an Indigenous people who live there.
fact: Himba women of Namibia are known for coating their skin and hair with otjize, a red paste of ochre and butterfat.

q: Match each food with its main ingredient.
fact: Tofu is made a bit like cheese: soy milk is curdled, and the curds are pressed into blocks.

q: Match each country with a cheese that comes from it.
fact: Under EU law only cheese made in Greece from sheep's milk, or sheep's and goat's milk, may be sold as feta.

q: Match each country with a traditional drink it is known for.
fact: In Morocco, mint tea is poured from high above the glass to give it a frothy top.

q: Match each country with the nickname of its flag.
fact: Hinomaru means 'circle of the sun', and Galanolefki simply means 'blue-white' in Greek.

q: Match each country with its national anthem.
fact: The Dutch 'Wilhelmus' is often called the oldest national anthem in the world; its tune dates from the 1500s.

q: Match each ocean with what sets it apart.
fact: The Pacific got its name from Magellan, who found its waters calm - 'pacific' means peaceful.

q: Match each continent with its highest mountain.
fact: Climbing the highest peak of every continent is a famous mountaineering challenge known as the Seven Summits.

q: Match each country with the largest island that lies entirely within it.
fact: Baffin Island in Canada's Arctic is the fifth-largest island in the world.

q: Match each country with the number of states or provinces it is divided into.
fact: Brazil's 26 states are joined by a Federal District, home to the capital, Brasília.

q: Match each strait with the lands on either side of it.
fact: At its narrowest the Strait of Gibraltar is only about 14 km wide, so Africa can be seen from Europe.

q: Match each Pacific country with its largest island.
fact: Tongatapu, home of the capital Nuku'alofa, is where nearly three-quarters of all Tongans live.

q: Match each Pacific country with one of its traditional dances.
fact: Tonga's lakalaka, in which long rows of dancers sing and move together, is on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage.

q: Match each country with what its people are called.
fact: In Lesotho one person is a Mosotho, many people are Basotho, and they speak Sesotho.

q: Match each country with the title of its monarch.
fact: Japan's emperor is the only reigning monarch in the world who holds the title of emperor.

q: Match each country with the name of its parliament.
fact: Ireland's parliament meets in Leinster House in Dublin, built in the 1740s for the family that became the Dukes of Leinster.

q: Match each country with the name it calls itself in its own language.
fact: Albania's own name, Shqipëria, is often linked to 'shqiponjë', the Albanian word for eagle.

q: Match each country with a leader honored as its founding father.
fact: Atatürk, meaning 'Father of the Turks', was a surname given to Mustafa Kemal by the Turkish parliament in 1934.

q: Match each event with the year it happened.
fact: The Channel Tunnel runs about 50 km between England and France, much of it deep under the seabed.

q: Match each country with a natural wonder found there.
fact: Ha Long Bay in Vietnam is dotted with nearly 2,000 limestone islands and islets rising straight out of the sea.

q: Match each famous street or square with its city.
fact: At Shibuya Crossing in Tokyo, the traffic lights stop all cars at once and thousands of people cross from every direction.

q: Match each animal with the continent where it lives in the wild.
fact: Bald eagles live only in North America, from Alaska and Canada down to northern Mexico.

q: Match each inventor with their invention.
fact: Louis Braille was only 15 when he worked out his alphabet of raised dots, which blind people still read today.

q: Match each country with an export it is famous for.
fact: Sri Lanka's tea is still sold around the world as Ceylon tea, after the island's old name.

q: Match each city of the highlighted country with a landmark found there.
fact: Florence's Ponte Vecchio has been lined with shops since the Middle Ages; today they are mostly jewelers.

q: Match each state of the highlighted country with its nickname.
fact: Texas is the Lone Star State after the single star on its flag, a reminder of its years as an independent republic.

q: Match each province of the highlighted country with its capital.
fact: Neither Vancouver nor Calgary is a provincial capital, even though each is the biggest city of its province.

q: Match each main island of the country shown with its largest city.
fact: Sapporo hosted the Winter Olympics in 1972 and is famous for its snow festival of giant ice sculptures.

q: Match each city of the highlighted country with what it is famous for.
pairs: Karst hills on the Li River
fact: Xi'an was once the eastern end of the Silk Road and served as China's capital for many dynasties.

q: Match each nation of the highlighted country with its capital.
fact: Cardiff only became the capital of Wales in 1955, which makes it one of Europe's youngest capital cities.

q: Match each city in the highlighted country with its best-known landmark.
fact: Segovia's Roman aqueduct, about 2,000 years old, was built from granite blocks held together without any mortar.

q: Match each town of the highlighted country with what draws visitors there.
fact: The world's first commercial bungee jump opened in 1988 on the Kawarau Bridge near Queenstown.

q: Match each place in the highlighted country with what it is known for.
fact: Tutankhamun's tomb was found almost untouched in the Valley of the Kings in 1922.
